c: Course 1. Identity, Purpose and Values.
An effective leader starts by identifying the gifts, limits and values she brings to service.
A title is not an identity: it is a responsibility.
Encourage learners to notice specific evidence of their contribution, listen to feedback and connect aspirations with WODDI-approved opportunities.
Lesson 1.1. Knowing Your Strengths.
A strength is a repeatable ability that helps you contribute well.
Observe when you solve problems effectively, ask trusted peers for specific examples, and distinguish a demonstrated skill from a title.
A leader should use strengths responsibly and continue developing weaker areas.
Here is an example.
A chapter volunteer who organises attendance reliably may support meeting coordination while learning facilitation skills.
Your practice:
List three demonstrated strengths, one example of each, and one skill you want to improve.
Lesson 1.2. Values and Integrity.
Values are standards guiding choices when nobody is watching.
Integrity requires consistency between commitments, decisions and actions.
Leaders must honour confidentiality, fairness and WODDI rules, and promptly disclose conflicts that could affect decisions.
Here is an example.
A coordinator refuses to favour a friend for a role and refers candidates through the approved HQ screening process.
Your practice:
Write five personal values and describe one observable behaviour for each.
Lesson 1.3. Discovering Purpose.
Purpose connects a person's abilities to meaningful needs.
It can develop as circumstances change.
A practical purpose statement identifies who you hope to serve, what contribution you can make and the values that guide your actions.
Here is an example.
A volunteer chooses to mentor new members because she enjoys helping others learn practical skills.
Your practice:
Draft a one-sentence service purpose statement and ask a peer to review it.
Lesson 1.4. Personal Vision and Direction.
A vision is a clear picture of desired positive contribution.
Translate it into near-term steps that are within your control.
Separate personal aspirations from institutional commitments and check proposed work against approved programme priorities.
Here is an example.
A state leader plans to improve onboarding quality this quarter rather than promising unapproved nationwide expansion.
Your practice:
Write a six-month personal development vision and three achievable steps.
Lesson 1.5. Building a Personal Blueprint.
A personal blueprint combines goals, learning needs, service commitments and review points.
It should be specific enough to guide action yet flexible enough to adapt to feedback, capacity and changing circumstances.
Here is an example.
A leader schedules one course, one community activity and a monthly reflection, then revises the plan after reviewing progress.
Your practice:
Complete a one-page personal blueprint with goal, next step, support and review date.
Course 2. Confidence, Self-Worth and Resilience.
Confidence grows from preparation, practice and feedback rather than comparison.
Resilience does not require suppressing difficulty; it means responding constructively, using support and adjusting expectations after setbacks.
Leaders can model courage while making room for rest and help.
Lesson 2.1. Healthy Self-Confidence.
Confidence develops through preparation, practice and accurate self-assessment.
It does not require pretending to know everything.
A reliable leader can state what they know, ask questions and seek assistance when needed.
Here is an example.
Before facilitating a meeting, a volunteer rehearses the agenda and checks uncertain facts with HQ.
Your practice:
Prepare and practise a two-minute introduction to your volunteer role.
Lesson 2.2. Recognising Self-Worth.
Personal worth is not determined by a role, certificate or number of followers.
Leaders can respect themselves and others while acknowledging differences in experience and opportunity.
Equal dignity should shape volunteer interactions.
Here is an example.
A chapter leader values a new member's contribution even though the member has never held office.
Your practice:
Write three statements describing qualities beyond your volunteer title.
Lesson 2.3. Working Through Self-Doubt.
Self-doubt can signal uncertainty, not inability.
Break a challenge into manageable steps, gather reliable information and seek constructive guidance.
Review evidence rather than letting a single difficult moment define your ability.
Here is an example.
A volunteer nervous about presenting begins with a short five-minute briefing and builds experience gradually.
Your practice:
Identify a challenge, its first manageable step and one person who can provide feedback.
Lesson 2.4. Responding to Setbacks.
Resilience means adjusting after a setback and seeking support, not enduring unlimited demands.
Use a learning review: what happened, what was controllable, what needs changing and who can help.
Protect health and responsibilities outside volunteering.
Here is an example.
Low attendance prompts a team to check scheduling and reminders rather than blaming members.
Your practice:
Write a four-question learning review for a recent minor challenge.
Lesson 2.5. Courage and Constructive Initiative.
Courage in volunteering means raising concerns respectfully, acting within authority and taking small responsible steps.
Initiative should never bypass safeguarding, finance controls or HQ appointment processes.
Here is an example.
A volunteer identifies an underserved community and submits a proposal for approval rather than announcing a new programme.
Your practice:
Describe one improvement to propose through the approved channel.
Course 3. Discipline, Productivity and Time Management.
Productivity means delivering important commitments reliably, not appearing busy.
Distinguish urgent tasks from important results, allocate realistic time and communicate constraints early.
Reliable handovers are a sign of responsible leadership.
Lesson 3.1. Choosing Priorities.
Urgency and importance are different.
Identify work linked to agreed objectives, protect deadlines and distinguish essential deliverables from optional activities.
Reconfirm priorities with the responsible supervisor when demands conflict.
Here is an example.
A country leader completes overdue onboarding follow-ups before redesigning an optional flyer.
Your practice:
Rank five current responsibilities by impact, deadline and dependency.
Lesson 3.2. Planning Time Realistically.
Plan around available time, caregiving, employment and other commitments.
Break tasks into short steps and include buffer time.
Volunteers should be able to discuss realistic capacity without pressure to overcommit.
Here is an example.
A volunteer allocates two weekly hours for follow-ups instead of promising daily meetings she cannot attend.
Your practice:
Prepare a one-week voluntary service schedule with a realistic time limit.
Lesson 3.3. Building Helpful Habits.
Habits are easier to maintain when linked to a clear cue and a small action.
Start with a repeatable behaviour and review whether it improves service.
Avoid turning motivation into excessive monitoring.
Here is an example.
A leader checks WDOS tasks every Monday morning and updates progress in one session.
Your practice:
Choose one ten-minute weekly habit and define its trigger.
Lesson 3.4. Avoiding Procrastination.
Procrastination often grows when a task is unclear or overwhelming.
Define the next visible action, remove avoidable distractions and ask for clarification when needed.
Begin with the smallest meaningful step.
Here is an example.
Rather than delaying a report, a coordinator first gathers the attendance figures and confirms missing fields.
Your practice:
Break one delayed responsibility into three concrete actions.
Lesson 3.5. Accountability and Follow-Through.
Accountability includes honest status updates, evidence, deadlines and early escalation of blockers.
Distinguish completed, ongoing and delayed tasks.
Never mark work completed solely because a message was sent.
Here is an example.
A state leader uploads an attendance record and notes that one chapter report is still outstanding.
Your practice:
Create a task update with owner, deadline, status, evidence and blocker.
Course 4. Emotional Intelligence and Self-Management.
Emotional intelligence involves recognising the feelings that influence a response and choosing a respectful action.
It is particularly important in multilingual virtual teams where brief messages can be misread.
Emotional awareness should improve decisions without making assumptions about other people.
Lesson 4.1. Understanding Emotional Signals.
Emotions provide information about experience but do not automatically establish facts.
Notice changes in mood, physical tension and assumptions before responding.
Pause to understand what is known and what still needs clarification.
Here is an example.
A coordinator notices frustration after a late report and checks the reason before responding.
Your practice:
Describe a common stressful situation and one question to check your assumptions.
Lesson 4.2. Regulating Responses.
Self-regulation involves choosing a proportionate response even when a situation is uncomfortable.
Short pauses, clear language and requesting a better time to discuss a matter can prevent unnecessary conflict.
Here is an example.
A deputy drafts a calm follow-up rather than replying harshly to a misunderstood message.
Your practice:
Rewrite a tense message into a factual and respectful response.
Lesson 4.3. Practising Empathy.
Empathy seeks to understand another person's perspective without assuming or excusing harm.
Ask open questions, listen and recognise that members face different resources and constraints.
Here is an example.
A leader learns that a volunteer missed training due to connectivity problems and offers an alternative route.
Your practice:
Write two open-ended questions to understand a struggling volunteer's situation.
Lesson 4.4. Receiving Feedback Well.
Constructive feedback focuses on observable behaviour and improvement.
Listen for specifics, ask questions and decide an appropriate action.
Feedback should never become humiliation or personal attack.
Here is an example.
A leader asks which part of a report was unclear and revises the format.
Your practice:
Write a three-part response: appreciation, clarification, next step.
Lesson 4.5. Healthy Boundaries and Support.
Volunteer responsibility should be sustainable.
Clearly communicate availability, respect privacy, avoid taking on specialist counselling roles and refer serious concerns through appropriate channels.
Boundaries help preserve trust and quality of service.
Here is an example.
A volunteer leader explains her availability and directs a member needing specialised support to a qualified service.
Your practice:
Draft a polite boundary-setting message about response hours.
Course 5. Communication, Facilitation and Public Speaking.
Communication succeeds when the listener knows the purpose, action, owner and deadline.
Good facilitation invites participation, summarises decisions and documents follow-up.
Virtual and cross-cultural communication calls for plain language and accessible formats.
Lesson 5.1. Active Listening.
Active listening means allowing a speaker to finish, asking clarifying questions and accurately reflecting the key point.
Distinguish what was said from what you assumed.
Follow up with a short agreed action summary.
Here is an example.
A meeting chair restates a member's concern before proposing a solution.
Your practice:
Practise summarising a colleague's point in two neutral sentences.
Lesson 5.2. Professional Written Communication.
Professional messages state purpose, relevant context, requested action and deadline politely.
Use precise dates and avoid unnecessary personal data.
Written instructions should be understandable to people using different devices or languages.
Here is an example.
An HQ task note says what to submit, approved format and deadline, instead of simply saying “urgent”.
Your practice:
Draft a four-sentence task request with a clear deadline and submission method.
Lesson 5.3. Public Speaking Basics.
An effective short address has a clear opening, two or three main points and an actionable close.
Practise pace and pronunciation, and check facts before speaking on behalf of WODDI.
Avoid implying authority you do not hold.
Here is an example.
A regional leader delivers a three-minute orientation on approved volunteer duties.
Your practice:
Draft and rehearse a three-minute message with one call to action.
Lesson 5.4. Facilitating Inclusive Meetings.
A facilitator creates an agenda, invites balanced contributions, manages time and documents decisions.
Provide suitable ways for quieter participants to contribute and accommodate connectivity limits where feasible.
Here is an example.
A chapter meeting uses a short agenda and a written channel for members unable to speak live.
Your practice:
Create a 20-minute agenda with participation and action-summary slots.
Lesson 5.5. Cross-Cultural Digital Communication.
WODDI operates across languages and regions.
Use plain respectful language, confirm meanings, avoid stereotypes and check time zones.
Do not assume translation tools are always accurate; confirm critical information.
Here is an example.
A continental notice includes the correct WAT time and asks leaders to confirm local time.
Your practice:
Rewrite a meeting notice in plain language with clear date, time and location format.
Course 6. Ethical Leadership and Service.
Service leadership is measured by fair process and dependable conduct, not personal control.
Use clear role boundaries, disclose conflicts of interest and protect trust.
WODDI leader referrals move through approved HQ screening and appointment, rather than informal promises.
Lesson 6.1. Servant Leadership.
Service-oriented leadership focuses on enabling others, not collecting status.
It listens to needs, shares credit and models responsibility.
Titles are roles of service, not permission to control others.
Here is an example.
A chapter lead helps new volunteers understand an activity rather than treating questions as disrespect.
Your practice:
Identify one barrier you can remove for your team without exceeding authority.
Lesson 6.2. Decision-Making with Evidence.
Good decisions combine reliable facts, consultation, risk assessment and organisational rules.
When authority is unclear, seek direction before acting.
Record the reason for significant recommendations.
Here is an example.
A country representative checks verified membership data before recommending where to focus outreach.
Your practice:
Write a short decision note with evidence, options, risks and escalation point.
Lesson 6.3. Delegation and Teamwork.
Delegation matches tasks to capacity and clarity.
Agree on output, due date, support and reporting.
Delegating does not mean abandoning accountability or shifting an unreasonable workload.
Here is an example.
A regional coordinator assigns two approved follow-ups with clear ownership and offers help with the dashboard.
Your practice:
Create an assignment with output, owner, due date and check-in.
Lesson 6.4. Ethics, Confidentiality and Data.
Volunteer leaders may encounter personal information.
Collect only authorised data, use approved systems and limit access by role.
Confidential information should not be circulated casually in chat groups.
Here is an example.
A chapter leader updates the approved WDOS record rather than posting members' phone numbers publicly.
Your practice:
List three data-handling boundaries for your role.
Lesson 6.5. Authority, Referral and HQ Controls.
Within WODDI, leaders may identify and refer potential volunteers, while HQ manages screening and appointment.
Volunteers must not create unauthorised accounts, collect levies or commit the organisation to agreements.
Here is an example.
A state coordinator submits a candidate through WDOS and waits for the HQ appointment process.
Your practice:
Map the steps from identifying a prospective leader to HQ decision.
Course 7. Financial Literacy and Resource Stewardship.
Personal financial literacy supports sustainable volunteer participation.
Distinguish needs from wants, use realistic plans and avoid high-pressure promises.
Institutional resources are separate from personal funds and must follow HQ authorisation and documentation procedures.
Lesson 7.1. Understanding Personal Cash Flow.
Cash flow is money received and money spent over a period.
Separate essential expenses, planned savings and discretionary spending.
Personal budgeting supports choices; volunteers should never be pressured to finance organisational activities privately.
Here is an example.
A volunteer plans transport costs without assuming that unpaid expenses must be absorbed personally.
Your practice:
Create a simple personal income-and-expense worksheet using hypothetical figures.
Lesson 7.2. Setting Financial Goals.
Useful financial goals name an amount, time frame and realistic actions.
Revisit goals when circumstances change.
Build habits that fit available resources rather than using arbitrary savings percentages for everyone.
Here is an example.
A member plans a modest emergency reserve with achievable contributions.
Your practice:
Write one short-term financial goal and two actions within a hypothetical budget.
Lesson 7.3. Spending and Consumer Choices.
Evaluate needs, total cost, alternatives and affordability before purchasing.
Beware of pressure, unclear fees and offers that appear too good to be true.
Comparison shopping should support informed decisions.
Here is an example.
A volunteer checks price, quality and transport cost before purchasing personal equipment.
Your practice:
Compare two hypothetical purchases using total cost and usefulness.
Lesson 7.4. Recognising Financial Scams.
Warning signs include guaranteed high returns, secrecy, pressure to act immediately and requests for passwords or verification codes.
Verify organisations independently, and never share sensitive credentials.
Here is an example.
A volunteer independently checks a suspicious investment pitch rather than forwarding it to the chapter.
Your practice:
Identify three red flags in a fictional suspicious financial message.
Lesson 7.5. Stewardship of WODDI Resources.
WODDI programme spending and commitments are HQ-controlled.
Volunteers should request approval, maintain evidence and report accurately.
Do not collect dues, create local accounts or sign contracts on behalf of WODDI without authority.
Here is an example.
A regional leader submits a cost proposal to HQ rather than collecting money from chapter members.
Your practice:
Prepare a hypothetical request containing purpose, cost estimate and approval requirement.
Course 8. Digital Literacy, WDOS and Online Safety.
Digital competence means using tools accurately, safely and inclusively.
A responsible WDOS user maintains accurate jurisdiction records, respects role permissions and flags issues promptly.
Data minimisation is especially important when records identify members or their locations.
The process in this course: Verify source, enter accurately, restrict access, check, report.
By the end of this course you should be able to explain the five ideas in your own words, tell good practice from common mistakes, complete a practical activity and make a realistic improvement plan.
Avoid sharing passwords, mass-downloading personal records or moving sensitive data to informal chat groups.
Lesson 8.1. Finding Your Way Around WDOS.
WDOS supports member records, approved volunteer tasks, communication, learning and reporting.
Access depends on assigned role.
Leaders should confirm their dashboard permissions and use official support when a feature is unavailable.
Lesson 8.2. Completing Digital Tasks.
Read task scope, deliverables, due date and upload rules before work begins.
Submit accurate evidence in the requested format and distinguish drafts from approved documents.
Ask for clarification before deadline when necessary.
Here is an example.
A chapter coordinator uploads a completed attendance summary as requested and marks remaining items pending.
Your practice:
Draft a sample task submission with status, evidence and blocker.
Lesson 8.3. Protecting Passwords and Accounts.
Use unique strong passwords and multi-factor authentication where available.
Beware of phishing links, unexpected login prompts and requests for codes.
Notify the official administrator promptly if an account may be compromised.
Here is an example.
A leader reports a suspicious password-reset email without opening its link.
Your practice:
Write a checklist for verifying unexpected account messages.
Lesson 8.4. Responsible Online Communication.
Digital messages can travel beyond their intended audience.
Check accuracy, permissions and tone before posting.
Use approved channels for official information and seek consent before sharing identifiable images.
Here is an example.
A volunteer checks image permissions and approved event details before posting a recap.
Your practice:
Draft a safe-event posting checklist covering facts, consent and approved branding.
Lesson 8.5. Using Data for Improvement.
Useful dashboards distinguish registrations, active participation and completed outcomes.
Check duplicates and data definitions before reporting trends.
Small datasets require caution; transparency matters more than impressive totals.
Here is an example.
A country leader reports 40 registered and 22 attended instead of claiming 40 participants.
Your practice:
Make a sample report with separate registered, attended and completed fields.
Course 9. Conflict Resolution, Collaboration and Boundaries.
Teams experience disagreement because priorities, resources and perspectives differ.
Resolve matters by listening, clarifying the issue, distinguishing facts from assumptions and agreeing the next step.
Boundaries support trust and prevent misuse of role authority.
Lesson 9.1. Understanding Conflict.
Conflict may arise from different expectations, limited information, competing priorities or disrespect.
Separate the issue from assumptions about character.
Recognise when a situation requires formal safeguarding or management escalation.
Here is an example.
Two coordinators disagree over a reporting deadline; they check the written instruction before debating motives.
Your practice:
Describe a hypothetical conflict using facts, interpretations and next step.
Lesson 9.2. Respectful Difficult Conversations.
Use specific observations, explain impact, listen and agree on next steps.
Address the behaviour, not the person's identity.
Choose a suitable private setting for sensitive feedback.
Here is an example.
A supervisor discusses repeated late updates privately and explores workload constraints.
Your practice:
Write a four-sentence respectful feedback script.
Lesson 9.3. Negotiating Shared Solutions.
Good negotiation explores underlying needs and feasible options.
A fair solution should respect rules, roles and capacity.
State where HQ approval is required rather than bargaining away an institutional rule.
Here is an example.
Two chapters agree to share a facilitator after HQ approves a revised timetable.
Your practice:
List two options for resolving a fictional scheduling clash.
Lesson 9.4. Collaboration Across Leadership Levels.
Country, state or regional, district, community and chapter roles need clear boundaries and consistent information flow.
Escalate issues through the appropriate structure, while urgent safeguarding concerns require prompt approved reporting.
Here is an example.
A ward leader shares verified updates with the district lead instead of issuing contradictory instructions to all chapters.
Your practice:
Draw a simple escalation and reporting path for your current position.
Lesson 9.5. Repairing Trust and Setting Boundaries.
Trust is rebuilt through accountability, changed behaviour and time, not an apology alone.
Maintain appropriate boundaries and do not pressure others to reconcile immediately.
Serious allegations require formal processes, not informal mediation alone.
Here is an example.
A leader acknowledges a missed commitment, corrects the record and establishes a check-in process.
Your practice:
Write a repair plan with acknowledgement, corrective action and review.
Course 10. Wellbeing, Balance and Sustainable Volunteering.
Sustainable service depends on realistic expectations and a culture that respects volunteers’ other responsibilities.
Leaders should model breaks, shared tasks and timely communication.
Encourage practical support without turning colleagues into counsellors.
Lesson 10.1. Recognising Stress and Workload.
Stress may appear as difficulty focusing, irritability or fatigue.
These signs are not diagnoses.
Review workload, responsibilities and available support, and take persistent concerns seriously.
Here is an example.
A volunteer facing overlapping deadlines informs the supervisor and renegotiates tasks.
Your practice:
Make a personal workload map showing essential duties, capacity and help needed.
Lesson 10.2. Rest, Routines and Recovery.
Regular rest, movement, nourishment and social connection can support wellbeing.
There is no universal routine that suits every person.
Volunteer expectations should allow for life responsibilities and recuperation.
Here is an example.
A chapter coordinator schedules the next meeting at a sustainable time rather than holding daily late-night calls.
Your practice:
Design a balanced weekly routine with rest and volunteer time.
Lesson 10.3. Seeking Appropriate Support.
Volunteers can listen respectfully but should not act as clinicians or counsellors without qualifications.
Encourage appropriate professional or trusted support when a concern exceeds the volunteer role; follow safeguarding policy where applicable.
Here is an example.
A leader supports a member in finding an appropriate qualified service without attempting diagnosis.
Your practice:
List your support boundaries and approved escalation contacts to confirm with HQ.
Lesson 10.4. Work-Life-Volunteer Boundaries.
Healthy boundaries make commitments clear and manageable.
Agree response expectations and check-in methods.
Taking leave or changing capacity is not evidence of poor character.
Here is an example.
A volunteer informs the team in advance about an examination week and arranges an approved handover.
Your practice:
Write an availability statement and a simple handover plan.
Lesson 10.5. A Culture of Care.
A caring team welcomes questions, avoids humiliation and notices exclusion.
Check in without intruding into private life.
Evaluate systems and workload rather than treating every delay as a personal weakness.
Here is an example.
A meeting facilitator offers an offline summary to a volunteer with inconsistent connectivity.
Your practice:
Suggest two inclusive changes to a fictional volunteer meeting format.
Course 11. Community Engagement and Impact.
Effective engagement begins with listening before announcing solutions.
A small approved activity with a clear beneficiary group, feasible resources and documented results can be more valuable than an unmeasured large event.
Capture feedback without overstating impact.
Lesson 11.1. Listening to Community Needs.
Begin with respectful listening rather than assuming what people need.
Gather suitable feedback and consider who is not represented.
Avoid promising programmes before WODDI approval and capacity checks.
Here is an example.
A leader asks members about learning access before proposing a digital training session.
Your practice:
Prepare five neutral questions for a community listening conversation.
Lesson 11.2. Inclusive Mobilisation.
Inclusive outreach respects language, accessibility, safety and local context.
Use invitations rather than pressure, and ensure participation is voluntary.
Offer alternatives where practical for people with connectivity or scheduling barriers.
Here is an example.
A state leader invites women's associations to nominate interested participants through an HQ-approved process.
Your practice:
Draft an inclusive invitation using clear eligibility and an approved referral path.
Lesson 11.3. Designing a Small Service Activity.
A sound proposal states the need, intended participants, outputs, safeguarding considerations, resources and approval process.
Start with feasible scope and define who owns each task.
Here is an example.
A community team proposes one approved skills-awareness session with a facilitator and attendance plan.
Your practice:
Complete a one-page activity concept note for HQ consideration.
Lesson 11.4. Measuring Outputs and Outcomes.
Outputs describe activities or direct products; outcomes describe the change those activities produce.
Track attendance honestly and avoid claiming long-term impact without evidence.
Use simple indicators suited to the activity.
Here is an example.
A training report records 35 attendance entries and a 10-question learning assessment, without claiming 35 new businesses.
Your practice:
Choose one output measure and one outcome measure for a sample workshop.
Lesson 11.5. Learning from Community Feedback.
Review participation, obstacles and feedback with the team.
Share honest findings and specific recommendations with HQ.
Close the loop by telling members what changed when appropriate.
Here is an example.
After low uptake, a coordinator tests a different meeting time before repeating the same format.
Your practice:
Write a mini after-action review: planned, happened, learned, next.
Course 12. Goal Setting, Mentorship and Leadership Readiness.
Personal development is a continuous loop of learning, practice and reflection.
Mentorship should support judgment and independence.
Consideration for new responsibility must rest on conduct, service evidence, role fit and HQ screening rather than certificates alone.
Lesson 12.1. Setting SMART Goals.
A useful goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Ensure it aligns with your actual volunteer capacity and role.
Describe evidence of completion rather than only intentions.
Here is an example.
A deputy commits to completing three approved onboarding follow-ups by a stated date and saving updates in WDOS.
Your practice:
Rewrite a vague ambition as a SMART personal development goal.
Lesson 12.2. Constructing a Development Plan.
A growth plan identifies priority skills, learning activities, practice opportunities, support and review dates.
It should include both technical and relational abilities.
Review what was learned, not only course completion.
Here is an example.
A volunteer chooses facilitation training and practises during a supervised chapter meeting.
Your practice:
Build a 90-day plan with two skills and one practice opportunity each.
Lesson 12.3. Mentoring and Peer Learning.
Mentoring creates structured opportunities to ask questions, reflect and learn.
Mentors should support independent judgement rather than direct every decision.
Agree on boundaries and protect sensitive information.
Here is an example.
An experienced state coordinator helps a new chapter leader prepare a meeting and then reflects on the experience.
Your practice:
Create a mentoring discussion agenda and two follow-up actions.
Lesson 12.4. Feedback and Growth Review.
A useful growth review compares planned actions with evidence, identifies improvements and sets the next step.
Include qualitative lessons and acknowledge external constraints.
Reviews should encourage development rather than punish low participation alone.
Here is an example.
A volunteer reviews meeting attendance together with accessibility barriers and adjusts outreach plans.
Your practice:
Prepare a monthly personal growth review with achievements, obstacles and next steps.
Lesson 12.5. Readiness for Greater Responsibility.
Leadership readiness combines reliable service, ethical conduct, learning, teamwork and willingness.
It does not automatically follow from passing quizzes.
HQ retains screening and appointment authority, and volunteers may choose to remain in non-leadership roles.
Here is an example.
A volunteer completes orientation, supports an approved project and is referred for HQ consideration without any promise of appointment.
Your practice:
Complete a leadership readiness reflection and list evidence, training needs and preferences.

In the WODDI Nurture NextGen Network, volunteer leaders are young people aged 18 to 29: students, graduates, apprentices and early-career workers who balance classes, exams, first jobs and family expectations, and who connect mostly online.
The goal is to turn this lesson into one observable behaviour: a clear decision, a helpful conversation, a documented action or a timely referral.
Learn the principle before applying it; do not substitute enthusiasm for evidence or authority.
How to apply it, step by step.
Step 1. Identify a current situation where this topic is relevant. Define the issue in one sentence rather than describing personalities.
Step 2. Note what you know, what you still need to confirm and who is affected.
Step 3. Choose a small response that fits your assigned role and WODDI procedures.
Step 4. Agree a reasonable next action, owner and check-in point.
Step 5. Record what happened and what you would improve.
What is the desired result in this situation?
What is within the leader’s control?
What could go wrong if she acts without listening, verification or approval?
What single next step would be most respectful, realistic and measurable?
Complete the exercise in four parts: (a) your current situation or starting point, (b) the improvement you want, (c) the action you will take, and (d) how you will know it worked.
Keep your answer short, and do not include unnecessary personal information about others.
What would you do differently in your current volunteer responsibility after studying this topic?
Write one concrete next action.
Learning evidence: record a dated example showing how you used this topic.
It can be a short reflection, a task record with no private details, or an action confirmed by your supervisor.
Here is an example.
A chapter mother who keeps attendance reliably helps coordinate the monthly meeting while she learns to lead discussions.
Your practice:
List three strengths you have shown at home, at work or in your community, one example of each, and one skill you want to grow.
Here is an example.
A campus chapter member who tracks attendance accurately helps run the meetings while she learns to facilitate.
Your practice:
List three strengths you have shown in class, at work or online, one example of each, and one skill you want to build this year.
Here is an example.
A ward coordinator refuses to favour her neighbour's daughter for a role and sends all candidates through the approved HQ screening.
Your practice:
Write five values that guide you as a mother and a leader, and one behaviour that shows each value.
Here is an example.
A chapter lead refuses to give a role to her course-mate as a favour and sends every applicant through HQ screening.
Your practice:
Write five values you want to be known for among your peers, and one behaviour that shows each value.
Here is an example.
A volunteer who loves teaching women practical skills chooses to welcome and guide new members of her chapter.
Your practice:
Write in one sentence who you want to serve, what you can give and which value guides you.
Ask a fellow member to read it.
Here is an example.
A graduate who enjoys explaining things volunteers to help first-year members understand how WODDI works.
Your practice:
Write one sentence on who you want to serve, what you can offer and which value drives you.
Ask a peer to review it.
Here is an example.
A state coordinator plans to improve how new women are welcomed this quarter instead of promising a national programme HQ has not approved.
Your practice:
Write a six-month picture of the leader you want to be and three steps you can take alongside your family responsibilities.
Here is an example.
A young state lead plans to improve how new members are welcomed this semester instead of announcing a national youth project HQ has not approved.
Your practice:
Write a six-month vision for your growth as a leader and three steps that fit around your studies or job.
Here is an example.
